flags.description: The SP + Type 4 combination produces the counter-type SP 4 — The Creative Individualist — whose hallmark is tenacity, forward drive, and refusal to show inner defeat rather than the more outwardly expressive melancholy of the standard Four. The client's own words confirm this: 'I just put my head down and push through… I'd rather prove I can endure than let anyone see me struggle' alongside a high Type 3 slider (61) and a tight grip on personal resources and routines.

stage0_analysis.notable_language: The idealization pattern is fully present: 'drawn to authenticity and beauty,' 'emotional depth and the ability to connect authentically with what is real and meaningful,' and 'very genuine and committed' (others' view) all map to the Four's 'I am unique, authentic, deep' self-image. The shadow is named with unusual directness: 'envy — a persistent sense that others have something I lack' is the Four's characteristic shadow stated plainly.

stage4_analysis.stress_point_description: The client picked the canonical Type 4 stress answer, pointing toward Type 2 territory under pressure — consistent with the Four's movement toward over-involvement, people-pleasing, or emotional entanglement when resources are depleted.
stage4_analysis.security_point_description: The client picked the canonical Type 4 security answer, pointing toward Type 1 territory when grounded — consistent with the Four accessing discipline, principled action, and constructive productivity when feeling safe.

holistic_analysis.stage0_coherence: The Stage 0 language is exceptionally clean for Type 4: 'feel things very deeply,' 'drawn to authenticity and beauty,' 'feeling misunderstood or like something essential is missing in me,' and the explicit naming of envy all track the Four's core motivation and shadow with high fidelity. No language in Stage 0 points meaningfully toward another type.
holistic_analysis.cross_stage_consistency: The SP instinct score (73) is the clear dominant, and the Stage 1 open response after the instinct sliders — 'managing my own resources… tight handle on my routines, my space, and my energy so I don't get caught off guard' — matches the SP 4 counter-type presentation precisely. The Stage 3 routing to counter-type mode was appropriate, and the Stage 3 lean resolved cleanly to Person A (Type 4). Stage 4 confirmed both stress and security points canonically. Every stage points the same direction.
holistic_analysis.instinct_coherence: SP dominates at 73 with a 22-point gap over SX (51) and a 33-point gap over SO (40). The instinct open response is a textbook SP anchor: resource management, self-reliance, routine, and not being caught off guard. Instinct confidence is high.
holistic_analysis.alternative_type_signal: Type 3 (the Performer) registered 61 on the slider and 48 in Call #1 coherence — elevated enough to note as the third candidate but not as a genuine alternate. The 'push through' and 'prove I can endure' language from the Stage 1 open text is better explained by the SP 4 counter-type pattern (tenacity, refusal to show weakness) than by a genuine Three motivation. The Stage 3 counter-type discriminating pair resolved cleanly to Four, ruling out a Three primary. The Type 1 alternate (Call #1 coherence 52) is structurally adjacent because Type 4's security point is Type 1 — but no 'I must be right/correct' worldview appears in Stage 0 language.
holistic_analysis.confidence_adjustment: Starting point is HIGH (CONFIRMED outcome). All five checks reinforce the hypothesis without qualification. The counter-type flag is a presentation nuance, not a confidence reducer — it actually clarifies why surface behaviors (push-through drive, high Type 3 slider) exist without displacing the Four core. Confidence remains HIGH.

client_facing.client_narrative:
What stood out immediately in your responses was the precision with which you named your inner life. 'I feel things very deeply,' 'drawn to authenticity and beauty,' and 'something essential is missing in me' — these are not approximations. They point toward a core orientation that is genuinely concerned with depth, meaning, and what is real.

And then there is this: 'envy — a persistent sense that others have something I lack.' The willingness to name that, clearly and without softening it, is itself a signature of the pattern we noticed.

The pattern that appears most consistent with what you described is Type 4 — The Individualist. This is the type whose deepest longing is for authenticity and a sense of completeness, and whose most persistent challenge is the feeling that something essential is always just out of reach.
client_facing.core_motivation_evidence:
The Four's core motivation is a longing for authentic selfhood — a search for identity and meaning that never fully settles, accompanied by a background sense of deficiency or incompleteness. Your description of 'something essential is missing in me' is one of the clearest expressions of this in the assessment data.

The way you named your greatest strength — 'emotional depth and the ability to connect authentically with what is real and meaningful' — aligns with the Four's orientation toward depth and genuine connection over surface presentation.

The explicit naming of envy as your most problematic quality is consistent with what the Enneagram tradition identifies as the Four's characteristic emotional habit: comparing inward and finding yourself wanting, while sensing others have what you lack.
client_facing.instinct_personal_overlay:
Your responses point toward the self-preservation instinct as the dominant lens through which your Four pattern operates. Where the Four's longing for something missing might manifest as intense emotional expression in other configurations, yours appears to turn inward toward endurance and self-management.

Your own words after the instinct questions describe it precisely: 'managing my own resources… a tight handle on my routines, my space, and my energy so I don't get caught off guard.' The ache of inadequacy is present — but the response is to hold the line, not to display the wound.

This combination is sometimes called the Creative Individualist, and it can look from the outside more like quiet determination than like the more expressive Four most people picture.
client_facing.secondary_type_narrative: The alternate hypothesis worth holding lightly is Type 1 — The Improver. Fours in their security movement access One energy — discipline, principled action, and an internalized standard of correctness — and for some Fours, especially in the SP configuration, this can read as a genuine One presentation. Your Stage 4 responses confirmed that you access One-like qualities when grounded and safe. Worth exploring with your Enneagram coach or practitioner: does the drive toward correctness and improvement feel like a resource you can access, or does it feel like your actual baseline?
client_facing.stress_point_narrative: Under significant stress, Fours can move toward Type 2 territory — becoming over-involved in others' needs, seeking connection or approval in ways that feel slightly unlike their usual self-reliant stance. You may notice yourself working harder to be needed, or finding it difficult to maintain your usual emotional boundaries when things are most difficult. Recognizing this movement for what it is — a stress response rather than a new problem — can help you find your footing again more quickly.
client_facing.security_point_narrative: When you feel genuinely grounded and supported, you have access to Type 1's positive qualities: focus, principled action, and the ability to translate what you feel into something disciplined and constructive. This is one of the Four's underappreciated resources. The path toward it often involves less looking inward for what's missing and more turning outward toward what actually needs to be done.
what_to_explore: At the center of the Four pattern is a longing for authenticity and completeness — a felt sense that something essential is missing, paired with a deep capacity for genuine connection and depth. Where do you notice this longing most vividly in your life right now? And what would you most like to explore with your Enneagram coach or practitioner about what it would mean to feel complete?

Think of a specific challenge you're currently navigating — something that is asking something real of you. How do your patterns of feeling deeply, comparing inward, and pushing through show up there? Are those patterns helping you, getting in the way, or doing both at once?

Some of the key strengths consistent with your pattern include emotional depth, authenticity, creative vision, and the capacity to stay committed under pressure. Some of the key challenges include envy, a sense of deficiency, and the difficulty of letting others see where you struggle. Which of these would you most like to bring more of — or work on — and what makes that one feel most alive right now?
instinct_evidence: You described keeping 'a tight handle on routines, space, and energy so I don't get caught off guard' — a self-preservation anchor.
You said you focus on 'not depending on anyone' and managing your own resources — consistent with SP self-reliance.
You described pushing through difficulty without letting anyone see you struggle — protecting your inner reserves.

coach_report.bottom_line: This is a high-confidence SP 4 — The Creative Individualist. The counter-type presentation is the single most important thing to hold going in: the client's push-through tenacity and resource-management focus can read as Three or One energy on the surface, but the Stage 0 language and Stage 4 confirmation leave no structural ambiguity about the Four core.

section1.the_read: This client is a clear SP 4. The Stage 0 language is unusually clean — 'something essential is missing in me,' 'envy — a persistent sense that others have something I lack,' 'drawn to authenticity and beauty' — these are not paraphrases of Four concepts; they are the concepts, stated in the client's own words. What complicates the surface read is the counter-type presentation: 'I just put my head down and push through… I'd rather prove I can endure than let anyone see me struggle' is textbook SP 4 tenacity, the hallmark of the Creative Individualist. The instinct open response — tight management of resources, routines, space, and self-reliance — further confirms the SP anchor. Stage 3 and Stage 4 both confirmed the Four hypothesis cleanly, with no ambiguity in the discriminating lean or the movement verification.
going_in: Confidence is HIGH — every stage of the assessment cohered; present the hypothesis with appropriate warmth and directness.

The counter-type framing is essential here: this client may not immediately recognize themselves in the more expressive or melancholic Four description. Lead with the SP 4 pattern — endurance, self-reliance, a private ache — not the dramatic or romantic archetype.
The client named envy explicitly and without softening. That's unusually self-aware. Honor that. Don't over-explain it — they know it.

Type 3 showed elevated on the slider (61) and the client's language includes performance-adjacent patterns ('prove I can endure'). The Stage 3 counter-type discrimination resolved this cleanly — but be ready for the client to recognize Three energy in themselves. That's the counter-type doing its work.
No self-typing was offered by the client. No contextual flags. The final open response field is absent.

why_this_matters: SP 4 is the counter-type: the Four pattern folds inward rather than outward.
Standard Four descriptions (expressive, romantic, melancholic) may not land — client may push back.
The counter-type's hallmark is tenacity and not-showing-weakness, not emotional display.
Mistyping risk: client may identify with 3 or 1 on the surface without counter-type framing.
standard_vs_counter: Standard Four: externalizes longing, drawn to intensity, comfortable displaying depth.
SP 4: internalizes longing, converts it into endurance, hides the wound behind capability.
Both share: the ache of deficiency, envy, hunger for authenticity, and depth of feeling.
The distinction is in the display — SP 4 'proves' rather than 'expresses.'
coaching_notes: Introduce SP 4 before the general Four description — don't make them work backward.
Anchor the counter-type in their own words: 'prove I can endure' is the key phrase.
Normalize the counter-type: this is still fully Four — the instinct just shapes the expression.

core_pattern: Type 4's core motivation: a longing for authentic selfhood, a felt sense of inner deficiency, and a search for what is missing — paired with a hunger for depth, meaning, and genuine connection.
The Four's worldview: 'I am fundamentally different, and something essential in me is lacking or lost — if I can find it, I will be whole.'
The core emotional habit is envy: the inward comparison that finds others complete and oneself perpetually incomplete.
Fours idealize what is absent and may devalue what is present — this is structural, not a character flaw.
what_responses_showed: 'Something essential is missing in me' — the deficiency belief stated with unusual directness.
'Envy — a persistent sense that others have something I lack' — the core emotional habit named plainly and without defensiveness.
'Drawn to authenticity and beauty' and 'emotional depth and the ability to connect authentically with what is real and meaningful' — the Four's idealization of depth and genuine contact.
'Creative, intense, self-absorbed at times, but very genuine and committed' (others' description) — the Four shadow (self-absorption) acknowledged alongside the Four strength (genuine commitment).
coaching_notes: This client already has significant self-awareness about the envy pattern — don't over-teach it. Move toward what it costs them.
The gap between what they feel inside and what they show outside is the SP 4 territory worth slowing down in.
Ask about the longing concretely — not 'do you feel something is missing' but 'what specifically feels missing right now?'
section2.probe: Try asking: When you say something essential feels missing — do you have a sense of what that something is, or does it stay just out of reach?

hardest_to_see: The SP 4 counter-type pattern means the client may not see their own emotional suffering — they convert it into endurance and forward drive, which can read (to them) as strength rather than as a defense.
'I'd rather prove I can endure than let anyone see me struggle' — this is both the strength and the shadow. The not-showing is where the Four isolation lives.
Envy is named but may be intellectualized. The felt-sense version — the moment it actually lands in the body when someone else gets the thing — may be harder to access in session.

framework_signals.label: Social Style — Withdrawing
bullets: Withdrawing types manage discomfort by moving away from contact — inward or into their own world.
For this client, withdrawal looks like self-containment: tight control of routines, not depending on anyone, not letting others see the struggle.
The withdrawal is not passivity — it is active self-protection. The client moves inward to manage, not to disengage from life.
framework_signals.probe: Weave in: When something really stings — when the envy or the sense of not-enough hits — where do you go? Do you move toward people or away?

framework_signals.label: Emotional Style — Intensity
bullets: Intensity types want to stay with what is real — they resist premature resolution and will hold the feeling rather than reframe it away.
For this client, intensity is internalized: the depth is real, but the SP instinct keeps it private rather than broadcast.
Watch for the client needing to feel that the pain has been fully honored before they can move. Don't rush to the reframe.
framework_signals.probe: Weave in: When someone tries to cheer you up or reframe a hard feeling — what happens inside? Does it land, or does it feel like something is being skipped?

framework_signals.label: Attachment Style — Frustration
bullets: Frustration types feel an ongoing sense that what they have is never quite what they need — the present is perpetually insufficient.
For this client, this shows up as the persistent ache that something essential is missing — a structural dissatisfaction, not a situational one.
The growth move for Frustration types is equanimity with the present — being in what is, not in the gap between what is and what should be.
framework_signals.probe: Weave in: Is there a version of your life that would feel complete — or does the sense of something missing seem to travel with you?

coaching_notes: This client works with frameworks well — they're self-reflective and articulate. Don't under-pitch the sophistication of the framing.
The shadow to name gently is the cost of the not-showing: what happens in relationships when nobody sees where they struggle?
The Intensity Harmonic means they need to feel met before they can move — don't try to coach them out of the feeling before naming it.
section3.probe: Try asking: Where do you actually feel the 'something missing' in your body — is it more like an ache, a tightness, an emptiness? Can you locate it right now?

how_instinct_shapes: SP 4 turns the Four's longing inward — not 'show the world my depth' but 'prove I can survive my depth.'
Self-reliance is the armor: managing resources, routines, and energy keeps the inner ache from being seen.
Envy goes underground — felt privately, rarely performed, sometimes converted into competitive drive.
This client's 'push through' pattern is the SP 4 hallmark: endurance as both strength and defense.
easy_to_miss: SP 4 looks like 3 on the surface — driven, capable, competent under pressure.
The Four depth is real but private; it won't announce itself the way SO or SX 4 does.
High Type 1 resonance is common: security point is One, and SP 4 can look principled and disciplined.
Counter-type: low resonance with standard Four description is expected, not a disconfirming signal.
coaching_notes: Name the counter-type early — it's disorienting to be told 'you're the dramatic one' when you're the one who never shows the struggle.
Anchor SP 4 in the client's words: 'prove I can endure' is the key phrase to return to.
Ask about what it costs to not be seen struggling — that's the growth edge.
section4.probe: Try asking: What would it mean — or cost — to let someone see you in the middle of the struggle, before you'd pushed through it?

stress_notes: Under stress, Type 4 moves to Two: seeking connection, becoming over-involved, losing self-reliance.
For SP 4, this is notable — the client who prides themselves on not depending on anyone may find themselves suddenly needing others.
Coach angle: normalize this as a stress signal, not a character change — it's the system asking for something.
section5.stress_probe: Try asking: When things get really hard — when the push-through isn't working — do you find yourself reaching for people more than usual? What does that feel like?
security_notes: In security, Type 4 moves to One: disciplined, principled, productive, engaged with what needs to be done.
For this client, this may feel like 'finally being able to act' — the feelings move into form.
Coach angle: One energy in security is a resource, not a new type — help them claim it.
section5.security_probe: Try asking: When you feel most grounded and supported, what becomes possible that isn't available when you're under pressure?
wings_notes: Three-wing (4w3): adds drive, performance energy, and ambition — amplifies the SP 4 tenacity and 'prove' dynamic.
Five-wing (4w5): adds withdrawal, intellectual depth, and a more reclusive quality — deepens the self-containment.
This client's elevated Type 3 slider (61) suggests a likely 3-wing, but let the client lead on which feels more natural.
Watch for the 3-wing intensifying the counter-type pattern — more achievement-oriented, more image-aware than a 5-wing Four.
section5.probe: Try asking: Do you find yourself more drawn toward achieving and being seen for what you accomplish, or more drawn toward understanding and being left alone to go deep?

bullets: When the client strongly recognizes the pattern, move quickly from recognition to specificity: which part resonates most, and when did they first notice it?
Use the envy acknowledgment as an anchor — they already named it. Ask what it would mean to relate to it differently.
Don't linger in the description — recognition is the beginning, not the destination. Ask what they want to do with it.
resonates_strongly.probe: What's one situation in your life right now where you can see this pattern most clearly — and what would you want to be different there?

bullets: Don't defend the hypothesis. Name the pushback as useful: 'What doesn't fit is as interesting as what does.'
If they identify more with Three: the drive and capability are real — ask whether the sense of something missing is also real, underneath the performance.
If they identify more with One: ask whether the standards and discipline feel like who they are, or like how they manage the ache.
Hold the counter-type frame gently: 'SP Fours often don't recognize themselves in the standard description — that's part of the pattern itself.'
pushes_back.key_distinction: The key question is: does the drive toward improvement come from an internalized standard of correctness (One) or from a persistent sense that something is missing in yourself that you're trying to overcome (Four)?

bullets: If the client is confused, find the foothold in what they named most clearly: the envy, the sense of something missing, the push-through.
Treat what doesn't fit as equally useful: 'The places where this doesn't land are worth exploring — what would be closer?'
Don't rush to resolve the confusion — sometimes sitting in the not-yet-knowing is itself a Four experience worth naming.
confused.probe: Which part of what we've talked about feels most like you — even if the rest doesn't fully land?

leading_quotes: I feel things very deeply, I'm drawn to authenticity and beauty, and I struggle with feeling misunderstood or like something essential is missing in me
envy — a persistent sense that others have something I lack
client_words.alternate_absence_note: The client's language shows no meaningful signal for Type 1 — The Improver: there is no orientation toward correctness, standards, or resentment about what is wrong, only the Four's characteristic longing and deficiency pattern.
